diagnosis.primary_pattern: Wind-Cold Obstructing Shaoyang Channels with Qi and Blood Deficiency
diagnosis.pathomechanism: COVID-19 infection severely depleted the patient's qi and blood reserves, weakening the defensive qi (wei qi) that normally protects against pathogenic invasion. Wind-cold pathogen subsequently invaded the Shaoyang (Gallbladder) channel, which supplies the facial nerve and ear region, causing channel obstruction. The pale tongue confirms profound qi-blood deficiency, while the white coating indicates residual cold-damp pathogen lodging in the channels. The floating-tense pulse reveals the body attempting to expel the exterior pathogen while simultaneously constrained by blockage and insufficiency. With depleted qi and blood unable to circulate effectively, facial nerve function becomes compromised—resulting in paralysis, numbness, and ear pain. This is acute-stage post-viral facial paralysis with favorable prognosis if properly addressed within the critical first 1-2 weeks.

constitution.characteristics: This patient normally would present as balanced or mildly yang-abundant at age 23, but COVID-19 has acutely depleted his qi reserves. The pale tongue and post-viral fatigue indicate significant qi insufficiency. His body is struggling to mount both defense against remaining pathogen and support tissue repair.
constitution.tendencies: Without proper recovery support, risk of: prolonged facial nerve recovery, chronic qi deficiency predisposing to recurrent infections, incomplete facial function restoration. Conversely, youth and timely intervention support rapid recovery.

analysis.summary:
This 23-year-old male presents with right-sided facial paralysis (House-Brackmann grade IV), numbness, and ear pain five days post-COVID-19—a classic presentation of post-viral Bell's Palsy understood in TCM as wind-cold obstruction of the Shaoyang (Gallbladder) channel combined with profound qi-blood deficiency. The pale tongue with white coating is diagnostic: the pale base reveals severe post-viral depletion of qi and blood production, while the white coat indicates cold-damp pathogen lodging in the channels. The floating-tense pulse confirms an exterior condition (virus still triggering defensive response) constrained by blockage (floating quality) and obstructed qi flow (tense quality).

The pathomechanism is clear: viral infection → qi and blood depletion → weakened defensive qi → wind-cold invasion of facial channels → circulation blockage → facial nerve paralysis. The right-sided unilateral involvement, ear pain (Gallbladder channel sign), facial droop, and numbness all point to Shaoyang channel obstruction. At day 5 post-onset and age 23, this is still the critical window for intervention—the nerve is damaged but not irreversibly so, and youth provides strong constitutional capacity for recovery.

Treatment must address both aspects simultaneously: expelling residual wind-cold pathogen while deeply tonifying qi and blood to restore circulation through the obstructed channels. This requires urgent medical oversight (to prevent corneal complications from incomplete eye closure and assess need for anti-viral or anti-inflammatory therapy), acupuncture to unblock channels and stimulate nerve recovery, herbal medicine to rebuild qi-blood circulation, strict eye protection, facial exercises to maintain muscle tone, and nutritional support focused on blood and qi tonification. Prognosis is favorable with comprehensive early intervention—spontaneous recovery rates for HB grade IV are 50-70% over 3-6 months; TCM intervention can significantly improve this timeline and completeness of recovery.

warning_signs: Worsening facial paralysis or drooping — indicates nerve damage progressing; requires immediate medical evaluation and possible EMG/NCS nerve testing
Eye pain, vision changes, or redness — indicates corneal damage from incomplete lid closure; ophthalmology emergency; risk of permanent vision loss
Fever, severe facial swelling, or signs of secondary infection — suggests bacterial superinfection; requires antibiotics and medical evaluation
Severe ear pain or fever with ear symptoms — possible otitis media or Ramsay Hunt syndrome complication; requires urgent medical assessment
Facial spasm or abnormal movements — may indicate aberrant nerve regeneration; requires specialist evaluation
contraindications: Do NOT apply heat (heating pads, moxibustion direct heat) to the face without professional guidance — can worsen acute inflammation in early phase and impair nerve recovery
Do NOT overexert facial muscles or aggressive massage — will increase swelling and damage partially functioning nerve fibers; gentle activation only
Do NOT ignore eye closure deficit — this is the most critical complication; incomplete closure leads to irreversible corneal scarring and blindness if unmanaged
Do NOT assume spontaneous recovery without medical monitoring — 30% of untreated HB grade IV results in permanent dysfunction; intervention in first 2 weeks critical
precautions.special_notes: This is Bell's Palsy (facial nerve paralysis) triggered by COVID-19 viral infection. TCM treatment is strongly complementary but CANNOT replace essential medical care: (1) Ophthalmology evaluation for eye closure adequacy is non-negotiable—if unable to close eye even partially, requires urgent protective measures (taping, protective glasses, frequent lubrication, protective ointment at night) to prevent blindness. (2) Medical assessment should exclude other causes of facial paralysis: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (varicella reactivation, often worse prognosis), Lyme disease (if in endemic area), temporal bone fracture, tumor, or stroke. These require different management. (3) Corticosteroids (prednisone) are most effective when started within 72 hours of symptom onset; at day 5 patient may still benefit if not yet started—discuss with physician. (4) Antiviral therapy (acyclovir, valacyclovir) may be considered for post-viral facial paralysis; discuss timing with medical team. (5) EMG/NCS testing can assess degree of nerve damage and help prognosticate (helpful at 3-4 weeks post-onset to guide expectations). TCM herbs, acupuncture, and supportive care significantly enhance recovery when combined with appropriate medical oversight. Prognosis for HB grade IV is good with comprehensive intervention: 50-70% spontaneous recovery, likely higher with active treatment.

follow_up.timeline: Reassess with TCM practitioner in 2 weeks (day 19); daily self-monitoring of: eye closure (most important), facial droop symmetry, sensitivity/numbness of facial skin, ear pain intensity. Medical follow-up with physician should occur at 1 week and 4 weeks minimum to monitor neurologic recovery.
follow_up.expected_improvement: Week 1-2: Some reduction in ear pain; improved sensation returning to numb areas; beginning return of eyelid closure (even partial improvement is positive sign). Week 2-4: Visible facial movement returning; ability to smile improving; droop decreasing noticeably; numbness regressing. Week 4-8: Significant motor recovery (may reach near-normal or complete recovery in this window with comprehensive treatment). Week 8-12: Fine motor control and facial symmetry normalizing; any remaining weakness from aberrant regeneration becoming apparent.
follow_up.next_steps: Continue acupuncture 2-3 times weekly for first 4-6 weeks, then 1-2 times weekly as improvement progresses. Continue herbal formula for 4-6 weeks minimum, reassessing at each 2-week mark. Maintain facial exercises, eye protection, and dietary support throughout recovery (minimum 3 months). If at week 3-4 showing minimal improvement despite compliance, request EMG/NCS testing to assess actual nerve recovery; may need to escalate medical intervention. Recovery trajectory should show clear week-to-week improvement; lack of progress warrants investigation for alternative diagnoses or complications. Long-term follow-up at 3-6 months to assess for aberrant regeneration (crocodile tears, synkinesis) and determine if additional treatment needed.

parsed.disclaimer: This Traditional Chinese Medicine diagnosis is complementary to—not a replacement for—professional medical care. Bell's Palsy is a medical condition requiring urgent ophthalmology evaluation to prevent vision-threatening complications, and medical assessment to exclude other causes of facial paralysis (Ramsay Hunt syndrome, Lyme disease, tumor, stroke). The TCM pattern differentiation provided here integrates available examination data to guide herbal and acupuncture treatment, which may significantly enhance recovery when combined with appropriate medical oversight. However, medical imaging, EMG/NCS testing, and medication management should be directed by licensed physicians. This assessment is based on limited examination data (tongue, pulse, symptom history) provided remotely and without in-person evaluation; a local TCM or medical practitioner should perform comprehensive assessment before starting treatment. All herbal formulas listed are traditional preparations requiring proper dosing by a qualified TCM herbalist; self-administration without guidance carries risk. Eye protection for incomplete eyelid closure is medically urgent and must be implemented immediately regardless of other treatments. Prognosis depends on degree of nerve damage, timing of intervention, and patient compliance with multi-modality treatment. This diagnosis serves as framework for discussion with your TCM and medical practitioners, not as definitive treatment prescription.
